tool.name: Dask
tool.tagline: Scale pandas, NumPy and plain Python to many cores and clusters
tool.description: Dask parallelizes Python analytics: it splits pandas DataFrames and NumPy arrays into many partitions or chunks, builds a lazy task graph, and runs it on all cores of a laptop or on a cluster of hundreds of machines. Its APIs mirror pandas and NumPy, and dask.delayed and futures parallelize arbitrary Python code. Learn it when your data or computation outgrows one core or one machine's memory but you want to stay in the PyData ecosystem.

glossary.def: A Python library that splits pandas, NumPy and plain Python work into many small tasks and runs them in parallel on all CPU cores of one machine or on many machines.
A large table made of many ordinary pandas DataFrames (partitions), used through the same methods as pandas but computed lazily and in parallel.
A large array made of a grid of NumPy arrays (chunks), used through the same functions as NumPy but computed lazily and in parallel.
One NumPy array piece of a Dask Array; the grid of chunks together forms the whole array.
Dask's recorded to-do list: every small step of work and which earlier steps it needs, built up lazily and run when you call compute().
One small unit of work in a Dask task graph, usually a function call on one partition or chunk.
The part of Dask that takes a task graph and decides which tasks run where and in what order.
Processing data that is bigger than the computer's memory by working on one piece at a time, so only a few pieces are loaded at once.
A tiny empty pandas DataFrame or Series that Dask keeps to know a result's column names and types without computing anything.
Moving every row to the partition where it belongs by some key, so rows that belong together end up together. The most expensive thing Dask does.
A placeholder for the result of a function call that Dask has recorded but not run yet; created by wrapping a function with dask.delayed.
Dask's full-featured scheduler: a scheduler process plus worker processes, on one machine or many, with a dashboard and memory management.
A scheduler and a few worker processes started on your own machine, usually by calling Client().
The object in your Python program that connects to a Dask scheduler, sends it work and fetches results.
A live web page served by the Dask scheduler that shows what each worker is doing, memory use and job progress.
The number of partitions in a Dask DataFrame.
The index boundary values between partitions of a Dask DataFrame, known only when the index is sorted; they let Dask skip partitions and join without shuffling.
Changing how many partitions a Dask DataFrame has, or how big they are, without changing the data.
The Dask DataFrame method that runs a function you write on each partition (a pandas DataFrame) in parallel.
Changing the chunk layout of a Dask Array; useful but expensive, since data must be moved between chunks.
The Dask Array method that runs a function you write on each chunk (a NumPy array) in parallel.
A handle to a task that has already been submitted to the workers and may still be running; call result() to wait for and fetch its value.
Sending a piece of data from your program to the workers once, so many tasks can use it without it being shipped with every call.
A merge where the small table is copied to every partition of the large one, so no shuffle is needed.
The distributed scheduler's default way of shuffling: workers send rows directly to each other piece by piece, with bounded memory and spilling to disk.
In Dask, to compute a collection and keep its pieces in the workers' memory for reuse, instead of bringing the result back to your program.
A worker moving some of the data it holds from memory to disk when memory is running low, to make room.
A small supervisor process beside each Dask worker that restarts the worker if it crashes or uses too much memory.
How Dask DataFrame records operations since 2025: each step is a node in a tree that Dask rewrites for speed before running it.
An optimization that reads only the columns a query actually uses, all the way back at the file reader.
An optimization that moves filters as close to the file reader as possible, so unneeded rows are skipped early.
Merging a chain of per-partition steps into one task, so the graph is smaller and less data is passed around.
The unique name of a task or value in a Dask task graph, such as a string or a tuple like ('sum-chunk-abc', 0).
The set of methods (__dask_graph__, __dask_keys__ and friends) an object must provide so dask.compute can handle it.
Dropping tasks from a graph that aren't needed for the results you asked for.
Running a task on the worker that already holds its input data, to avoid sending the data over the network.
An idle worker taking queued tasks away from a busy worker when that saves more time than moving the data costs.
The error Dask raises when a task has repeatedly caused its worker to be restarted, usually because the task used too much memory.
An object such as LocalCluster, KubeCluster or SLURMCluster that starts and stops a Dask scheduler and workers on a particular kind of infrastructure.
Letting the scheduler add workers when tasks are waiting and remove idle ones, within a minimum and maximum you set.

concepts.name: Lazy collections, partitions and compute()
concepts.summary: See how Dask cuts a big table into pieces, writes down the work instead of doing it, and runs it on all your CPU cores when you call compute().
concepts.why: Every part of Dask works this way, so understanding it explains both Dask's power and its surprises.
concepts.body:
pandas keeps a whole table in your computer's memory and works on it one step at a time. That stops working when the file is bigger than the memory you have, or when one step takes hours. **Dask** is a library that scales the tools you already know past those limits.

Its trick is to split the work into many small pieces. A **Dask DataFrame** is really a list of ordinary pandas DataFrames, each holding a slice of the rows; each slice is called a **partition**. In the same way, a **Dask Array** is a grid of NumPy arrays, each piece called a **chunk**. Each piece can be worked on separately.

Operations are **lazy**: nothing is calculated when you write them. `df.x.sum()` does not add anything up. It only records what would need to happen: sum each partition, then add the partial sums together. Each small step is a **task**, and the recorded to-do list, with each task pointing at the tasks it needs first, is called the **task graph**.

Calling `.compute()` hands the graph to a **scheduler**: the part of Dask that decides which steps run where and in what order. Steps that don't depend on each other run at the same time, in **parallel**, on the separate CPU cores of your laptop (or, later, on several machines). You get back a normal pandas or NumPy result.

This gives two benefits. Parallelism: many cores work at once instead of one. And **out-of-core** processing: only a few partitions need to be in memory at any moment, so the data can be bigger than your RAM, the working memory of your computer.

Rules of thumb:

- Call `compute()` once at the end, not after every step. Computing several results together, as in `dask.compute(a, b)`, shares the work they have in common.
- The result of `compute()` must fit in memory. Shrink it first (aggregate, filter), or write results to files.
- If your data fits comfortably in memory and pandas is fast enough, plain pandas is simpler. Dask pays off when data or compute time grow.
concepts.code:
import dask
import dask.dataframe as dd
import pandas as pd

pdf = pd.DataFrame({"x": range(10), "y": [1.0] * 10})
df = dd.from_pandas(pdf, npartitions=3)     # cut into 3 pandas pieces

print(df.npartitions)                      # 3
total = df.x.sum()                         # lazy: nothing added up yet
print(type(total).__name__)                # Scalar  (a Dask placeholder)
print(total.compute())                     # 45  (now the work runs)

mean_x, max_y = dask.compute(df.x.mean(), df.y.max())   # one shared pass
print(mean_x, max_y)                       # 4.5 1.0
takeaways: A Dask DataFrame is many pandas pieces (partitions) plus a recorded to-do list (the task graph)
Nothing runs until `compute()`; then the scheduler runs independent steps in parallel on all cores
Compute once at the end, and compute related results together with `dask.compute`
pitfalls: Calling `.compute()` on a huge DataFrame you haven't shrunk first, so the result doesn't fit in memory.

quiz.q: What does df.amount.mean() return for a Dask DataFrame df?
options: A lazy Dask placeholder you must compute()
quiz.explain: Dask operations are lazy: they return Dask objects that only describe the work until compute() is called.

concepts.name: Reading data into Dask DataFrames
concepts.summary: Create Dask DataFrames with read_parquet, read_csv and from_pandas, and inspect them with head, dtypes and npartitions.
concepts.why: How you load data decides partition sizes and column types, which drive everything that follows.
concepts.body:
A Dask DataFrame is usually created straight from files, so that each partition is loaded by its own task, and the tasks can run at the same time:

- `dd.read_parquet("data/*.parquet", columns=[...], filters=[...])` is the best option. A Parquet file stores the type of every column and a few summary numbers (like the smallest and largest value) for each block of rows. So Dask can read only the columns you ask for and skip blocks the filter rules out.
- `dd.read_csv("logs/2026-*.csv", dtype={"zip": "string"}, blocksize="64MB")` reads many files, or splits one big file into 64 MB blocks, each becoming a partition.
- `dd.from_pandas(pdf, npartitions=8)` cuts up a pandas DataFrame that is already in memory. Mainly for tests and demos, since the data had to fit in memory anyway.
- `dd.from_delayed` and `dd.from_map` build one partition per call of a function you write (a later lesson covers them).

Paths can be local, or point at files stored online in a cloud storage service (`s3://`, `gs://`, `abfs://`). Pass the login details for that service with `storage_options=`.

Some things are cheap to ask: `df.columns`, `df.dtypes` and `df.npartitions` are known without reading any data. That's because Dask keeps a tiny empty pandas DataFrame, called **meta**, that has the right columns and types and no rows. `df.head()` reads only the first partition. `len(df)` and `df.describe()` have to look at every row, so they can take a while.

CSV pitfall: a CSV file carries no type information, so Dask guesses each column's type from a sample at the start of the file. If later rows contain text in a column it guessed was numeric, a task fails halfway through. Pass an explicit `dtype=` for such columns, or better, convert once to Parquet with `df.to_parquet("out/")` and read that from then on.
concepts.code:
import dask.dataframe as dd
import pandas as pd

for i in range(3):   # three daily files
    pd.DataFrame({"day": [i] * 4, "zip": ["02134", "10001", "02134", "94105"],
                  "amount": [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]}).to_csv(f"sales-{i}.csv", index=False)

df = dd.read_csv("sales-*.csv", dtype={"zip": "string"})
print(df.npartitions)                    # 3  (one per small file)
print(df.dtypes.astype(str).to_dict())
# {'day': 'int64', 'zip': 'string', 'amount': 'float64'}
print(df.head(2)["zip"].tolist())        # ['02134', '10001']

df.to_parquet("sales_pq/")               # convert once, read fast later
pq = dd.read_parquet("sales_pq/", columns=["zip", "amount"])
print(pq.amount.sum().compute())         # 30.0
takeaways: Prefer `read_parquet` with `columns=` and `filters=`
`meta` gives columns and dtypes without reading data; `head()` reads one partition
Give CSV columns explicit dtypes, or convert to Parquet once
pitfalls: Letting Dask guess column types from the start of a messy CSV and getting failures halfway through a job.

quiz.q: Why does df.head() return quickly on a 500 GB Dask DataFrame while len(df) does not?
options: head() keeps a saved copy of earlier results
head() only reads the first partition; len() must count rows in every partition
quiz.explain: head computes just the first partition, whereas len needs a pass over all of them.

concepts.name: pandas-style operations in Dask
concepts.summary: Filter, assign, group and aggregate Dask DataFrames with the same methods as pandas, and know which parts of pandas behave differently.
concepts.why: Most Dask DataFrame code is ordinary pandas code; knowing the gaps keeps you from slow or failing patterns.
concepts.body:
Dask DataFrame offers most of the same methods as pandas, with the same names and arguments. Behind each call, Dask runs the pandas version on every partition, then adds a step that combines the per-partition results.

These work just like pandas: picking columns, boolean filtering `df[df.amount > 0]`, `assign`, arithmetic, the `.str` and `.dt` methods, `fillna`, `astype`, `isin`, and `value_counts`.

**Reductions and groupby** are done in a tree: first aggregate inside each partition, then combine the partial answers. `df.groupby("shop").amount.sum()`, `.agg({"amount": ["sum", "mean"], "id": "count"})` and `nunique` all work and are efficient when the number of groups is small. With many groups, pass `split_out=n` to spread the result over several partitions.

`groupby().apply(f)` is different: your function needs all rows of a group in one place. Rows of the same shop may sit in different partitions, so Dask must first move every row to the partition for its group. This all-to-all move is called a **shuffle**, and it is the most expensive thing Dask does. Prefer the built-in aggregations.

Differences from pandas:

- There is no `iloc` for picking rows by position, and `loc` needs a sorted index (see the partitions lesson).
- Some operations need to know the output columns and types up front, so they take a `meta=` argument.
- `sort_values` and `set_index` are expensive, because they shuffle the whole table.
- Results are lazy; call `compute()` to get pandas back, or `persist()` to compute and keep the Dask pieces in memory for reuse.
concepts.code:
import dask.dataframe as dd
import pandas as pd

pdf = pd.DataFrame({
    "shop": ["A", "B", "A", "C", "B", "A"],
    "amount": [10.0, -2.0, 5.0, 7.0, 3.0, None],
    "items": [2, 1, 1, 3, 1, 2],
})
df = dd.from_pandas(pdf, npartitions=2)

clean = df[df.amount > 0].assign(per_item=lambda d: d.amount / d["items"])
summary = clean.groupby("shop").agg(
    total=("amount", "sum"), n=("amount", "count"), avg_item=("per_item", "mean")
)
print(summary.compute().sort_index())
#       total  n  avg_item
# shop
# A      15.0  2      5.00
# B       3.0  1      3.00
# C       7.0  1      2.33...
print(df.shop.value_counts().compute().sort_index().tolist())   # [3, 2, 1]
takeaways: Most pandas column, filter and aggregation code runs unchanged
Groupby aggregations combine per-partition answers; `groupby().apply` shuffles rows between partitions
Avoid picking rows by position; it doesn't fit the partitioned model
pitfalls: Using `groupby().apply` with a custom function where a built-in aggregation would do.

quiz.q: Why is df.groupby('k').x.sum() cheap in Dask but df.groupby('k').apply(f) expensive?
options: sum runs on the graphics card
sum can be done per partition then combined; apply needs each group's rows together, forcing a shuffle
apply runs one partition at a time
quiz.explain: Sums can be combined from partial sums, while apply requires moving all of a group's rows into one partition.

concepts.name: dask.delayed: parallelize custom code
concepts.summary: Wrap ordinary Python functions with dask.delayed to build task graphs from loops and run the independent calls in parallel.
concepts.why: Many real workloads aren't DataFrames or arrays; delayed parallelizes any Python functions with a decorator.
concepts.body:
`dask.delayed` turns a function call into a lazy task. Calling a delayed function doesn't run it; it returns a **Delayed** object: a placeholder standing in for the result that will exist later. Passing Delayed objects into other delayed calls links them into a task graph.

```python
@dask.delayed
def load(path): ...
parts = [load(p) for p in paths]
total = dask.delayed(sum)(parts)
total.compute()
```

Dask sees that the `load` calls don't depend on each other, runs them at the same time, then runs `sum` when they are all done. You write a normal-looking loop; Dask finds the parallelism in it.

Guidelines:

- Decorate the **function**, then call it. Don't call the function and wrap the result: `delayed(f(x))` runs `f` immediately.
- Each task should do a meaningful amount of work, at least around 100 ms. Every task costs the scheduler a little bookkeeping time (its **overhead**), so a million tiny tasks is slower than a plain loop.
- Don't change the input objects in place, and don't read or write global variables inside a task. A task may run in another process, or on another machine, where those changes would be lost or invisible.
- Collect everything with one `dask.compute(*objs)` call.
- `total.visualize()` draws the graph as a picture (needs the graphviz package installed).

Delayed objects support attribute access, indexing and arithmetic; each becomes another task. You can turn a list of Delayed objects into a collection with `dd.from_delayed` or `da.from_delayed`.
concepts.code:
import threading
import time
import dask

threads_used = set()

@dask.delayed
def fetch(i):
    threads_used.add(threading.current_thread().name)
    time.sleep(0.5)            # pretend this is a slow download
    return i * 10

@dask.delayed
def combine(values):
    return sum(values)

parts = [fetch(i) for i in range(4)]   # nothing runs yet
total = combine(parts)

print(total.compute(num_workers=4))    # 60
print(len(threads_used) > 1)
# True: the fetches ran on several threads at the same time
takeaways: `@dask.delayed` makes calls lazy; passing Delayed objects builds a graph
Independent calls run in parallel when you `compute()`
Keep tasks coarse (around 100 ms or more) and don't change anything outside the task
pitfalls: Writing `delayed(f(x))`, which calls f immediately, instead of `delayed(f)(x)`.

options: process(data) runs immediately; only its result is wrapped
quiz.explain: Wrap the function first, delayed(process)(data), so the call itself becomes a task.

concepts.name: Schedulers and the distributed Client
concepts.summary: Choose between the threaded, process, synchronous and distributed schedulers, start a local Client, and open the dashboard.
concepts.why: The scheduler decides how fast your code runs and whether you can see what it is doing.
concepts.body:
The same Dask graph can be run by different **schedulers**. The simple ones live inside your own Python process:

- **threads** (the default for DataFrame and Array): runs tasks on several threads of your process. Great when the work releases the GIL, as most NumPy and pandas operations do, so the threads truly run at the same time.
- **processes**: runs tasks in several separate Python processes. Helps pure-Python code, which holds the GIL and so can't share one process. The cost: every input and result must be turned into bytes and copied between processes (pickled).
- **synchronous**: runs everything one task at a time, in the same thread as the rest of your program. Nothing is parallel, but errors show a readable traceback and you can step through a task line by line with `pdb` to find a bug.

Pick one with `dask.config.set(scheduler="threads")` or per call, `compute(scheduler="processes")`.

The fourth option is the **distributed** scheduler from the `dask.distributed` package. Despite the name, it is the best choice for anything non-trivial even on a laptop. `from dask.distributed import Client; client = Client()` starts a **LocalCluster**: a small scheduler process plus a few **worker** processes on your machine that execute tasks, and makes it the default. The same **Client** can later connect to workers spread over many machines.

What it adds: smarter task placement, moving data to disk when memory runs low, futures (a later lesson), and the **dashboard**. The dashboard is a web page (open `client.dashboard_link`, usually `http://127.0.0.1:8787`) that shows live what each worker is doing, how much memory it uses and how far the job has progressed. It is the single best tool for understanding performance.

`Client(n_workers=4, threads_per_worker=2, memory_limit="4GB")` sets the resources. In a script, create the Client under `if __name__ == "__main__":`, because each worker process imports your file again on start-up and would otherwise start its own cluster. Close it with `client.close()` or a `with` block.
concepts.code:
import dask
import dask.array as da
from dask.distributed import Client, LocalCluster

if __name__ == "__main__":   # worker processes import this file again
    x = da.ones((4000, 4000), chunks=(1000, 1000))
    with dask.config.set(scheduler="synchronous"):   # one task at a time
        print(x.sum().compute())                    # 16000000.0
    print(x.sum().compute(scheduler="processes"))   # 16000000.0

    with LocalCluster(n_workers=2, threads_per_worker=2, processes=True) as cluster, \
         Client(cluster) as client:
        print(len(client.scheduler_info()["workers"]))   # 2
        print("dashboard at", client.dashboard_link)    # http://127.0.0.1:8787/status
        print((x + x.T).mean().compute())               # 2.0  (runs on the workers)
takeaways: Threads by default; processes for pure-Python code that holds the GIL; synchronous for finding bugs
`Client()` starts a local scheduler and workers, and gives you the dashboard
Guard Client creation with `if __name__ == "__main__":` in scripts
pitfalls: Using the process scheduler for NumPy-heavy work and paying the cost of copying data between processes for nothing.

quiz.q: Your Dask code fails deep inside a task and you want to step through it with pdb. Which scheduler?
quiz.explain: The synchronous scheduler runs everything in your main thread, one task at a time, so debuggers and tracebacks work normally.

concepts.name: Partitions, divisions and the index
concepts.summary: Size partitions sensibly, use repartition, and understand divisions and set_index for fast loc lookups and joins.
concepts.why: Partition size and a sorted index are the two biggest levers on Dask DataFrame performance.
concepts.body:
**Partition size** matters. Each partition is a pandas DataFrame processed by one task. If partitions are too small (a few MB), the scheduler spends more time on bookkeeping per task than on the work itself. If they are too large (several GB), a worker can't hold a partition and its intermediate results in memory, and the job fails. Aim for roughly **100 MB to 1 GB in memory** per partition. Fix bad sizes with `df.repartition(partition_size="200MB")` or `npartitions=n`, especially after a filter that removed most rows and left many nearly empty partitions.

**Divisions** are what Dask knows about the index. If the index is sorted across partitions, `df.divisions` holds the boundary values, such as `(0, 1000, 2000, 2999)`, meaning partition 0 holds index 0 to 999 and so on. When divisions are known, Dask can:

- answer `df.loc["2026-03-01":"2026-03-07"]` by reading only the partitions whose range overlaps,
- join or align two tables on the index without a shuffle, partition against partition,
- do time-based operations such as resampling (regrouping rows into days or weeks) and rolling windows (statistics over the last n rows) correctly across partition boundaries.

If divisions are unknown, `df.known_divisions` is False and `df.divisions` is all None.

`df.set_index("timestamp")` sorts the whole dataset by that column and computes divisions. That's a full shuffle, so do it once and save the result to Parquet; later, `read_parquet(..., calculate_divisions=True)` can recover the divisions from the summary statistics stored in the files. If the data is already sorted, pass `sorted=True` to skip the shuffle.
concepts.code:
import dask.dataframe as dd
import pandas as pd

pdf = pd.DataFrame({"ts": pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=60, freq="D"),
                    "v": range(60)})
df = dd.from_pandas(pdf, npartitions=6, sort=False)
print(df.known_divisions)                 # False

indexed = df.set_index("ts", sorted=True)   # already sorted: no shuffle
print(indexed.known_divisions, indexed.npartitions)   # True 6
print(indexed.divisions[:2])
# (Timestamp('2026-01-01 00:00:00'), Timestamp('2026-01-11 00:00:00'))

week = indexed.loc["2026-02-01":"2026-02-07"]   # touches only 1 partition
print(week.npartitions, week.v.sum().compute())      # 1 238

small = indexed[indexed.v % 10 == 0].repartition(npartitions=1)
print(small.npartitions)                  # 1
takeaways: Target roughly 100 MB to 1 GB of memory per partition
Known divisions enable fast `loc`, index joins and time-series ops
`set_index` is a costly shuffle: do it once and save to Parquet
pitfalls: Keeping thousands of tiny partitions after a filter that dropped most rows, instead of repartitioning.

quiz.q: What do known divisions let Dask do with df.loc['2026-03-01':'2026-03-02']?
options: Read only the partitions whose index range overlaps the slice
Load the data into a GPU
quiz.explain: Divisions are the partition boundaries, so Dask can skip partitions outside the requested range.

concepts.name: map_partitions and meta
concepts.summary: Run any pandas function on every partition with map_partitions, and give Dask the output schema with meta.
concepts.why: When the pandas API in Dask doesn't cover what you need, map_partitions lets you use any pandas code in parallel.
concepts.body:
`df.map_partitions(func, *args, **kwargs)` calls `func` on each partition (a pandas DataFrame) and stitches the results back into a Dask DataFrame or Series. Anything you can do to a pandas DataFrame, including calling other libraries, can run in parallel this way.

Dask must know the output's columns and dtypes **before** running anything, so it builds an empty sample called **meta**. By default it calls your function on a tiny fake partition to guess. That can fail or guess wrong, for example when the function relies on real values. Pass `meta=` explicitly:

- for a DataFrame: `meta={"a": "int64", "b": "string"}` or an empty `pd.DataFrame` with the right dtypes
- for a Series: `meta=("name", "float64")`

Important: the function sees **one partition at a time**. It must not need rows from other partitions. A per-row cleanup, a vectorized feature or a model's `predict` are fine. A global rank, a running total across partitions, or a groupby that assumes all of a group is present are not, unless the data is partitioned by that key.

`map_partitions` is also a good place for setup cost you want once per partition rather than per row, like preparing a text-matching pattern or loading a small lookup table. Related helpers: `df.map_overlap` for windows that need neighbouring rows, and `df.partitions[i]` to select single partitions.
takeaways: `map_partitions` runs any pandas function on each partition in parallel
Pass `meta=` so Dask knows the output schema without guessing
The function must not need rows from other partitions
pitfalls: Computing a global statistic (like a rank or z-score) inside map_partitions, which only sees one partition.

quiz.q: Inside map_partitions you compute x - x.mean(). What mean is used?
options: The mean of x within each partition
It raises because mean is not allowed
quiz.explain: The function only sees one partition, so x.mean() is that partition's mean, which is usually a bug.

concepts.name: Dask Array: chunked NumPy
concepts.summary: Build chunked arrays with dask.array, choose chunk sizes, and run NumPy-style math, reductions and rechunking.
concepts.why: Dask Array scales NumPy code to arrays larger than memory, such as climate, imaging and simulation data.
concepts.body:
A **Dask Array** is a grid of NumPy arrays (chunks) that you use through the same functions and methods as NumPy: `da.ones`, `da.random.default_rng().random(...)`, `da.from_array(numpy_or_h5py_or_zarr, chunks=...)`, `da.from_zarr(path)`. Element-wise math, broadcasting, slicing, reductions with `axis=`, `matmul`, many `linalg` functions and NumPy ufuncs all work, lazily.

**Chunks** are the key design choice:

- Aim for chunks of roughly 100 MB (for example `(4000, 4000)` float64 is 128 MB). `chunks="auto"` picks a size for you.
- Align chunks with how you access data: if you mostly read one row at a time (say, one sensor's measurements over time), chunk so each row sits in few chunks.
- Operations that combine many chunks, such as transposes and some reductions, cost communication.

`x.rechunk((1000, -1))` changes chunking (`-1` means the whole axis in one chunk); it's expensive, so do it once and deliberately. `x.chunks` and `x.chunksize` show the layout, and printing an array in a notebook shows a helpful diagram of the chunks.

For custom per-chunk logic, use `x.map_blocks(func)`, or `da.map_overlap` when each chunk needs a border of neighbouring values, as in image filters and stencils. Store big results with `x.to_zarr(path)` rather than computing them into memory.
concepts.code:
import dask.array as da
import numpy as np

rng = da.random.default_rng(42)
x = rng.random((20_000, 5_000), chunks=(5_000, 5_000))   # ~800 MB, 4 chunks
print(x.numblocks, x.chunksize)       # (4, 1) (5000, 5000)
print(round(x.nbytes / 1e6))          # 800

col_means = x.mean(axis=0)            # lazy reduction
centered = x - col_means              # broadcasting, still lazy
print(np.allclose(centered.mean(axis=0).compute(), 0, atol=1e-9))   # True

y = x.rechunk((1_000, -1))            # whole rows per chunk
print(y.numblocks)                    # (20, 1)

z = x[:4, :3].map_blocks(np.round, 2)
print(z.compute().shape)              # (4, 3)
takeaways: A Dask Array is a grid of NumPy chunks with the NumPy API
Chunks of around 100 MB aligned with your access pattern work best
`rechunk` is expensive; `map_blocks` and `map_overlap` run custom code per chunk
pitfalls: Creating millions of tiny chunks (e.g. chunks=(10, 10)): the per-task bookkeeping then dwarfs the actual math.

quiz.q: A 40 GB array is chunked as (100, 100) float64 chunks (80 KB each). What is the likely problem?
options: Chunks are too large for memory
Nothing; small chunks are always faster
There are millions of tasks, so scheduling overhead dominates
quiz.explain: Tiny chunks create a huge graph; each task costs scheduler time far exceeding its compute.

concepts.name: Futures: real-time task submission
concepts.summary: Submit work immediately with client.submit and client.map, gather results, and react as tasks finish with as_completed.
concepts.why: Futures handle dynamic workloads where the next task depends on earlier results, which lazy graphs can't express.
concepts.body:
With the distributed Client you can also run tasks **eagerly**: work starts the moment you ask for it, instead of waiting for a `compute()`. `future = client.submit(func, *args)` starts work on the workers right away and returns a **Future**: a handle to a result that lives on a worker. `client.map(func, iterable)` submits many at once.

- `future.result()` waits and brings the value back; `client.gather(futures)` does it for a list.
- Passing a Future as an argument to another `submit` sends the dependency without bringing data back to your machine. The worker fetches it directly.
- `as_completed(futures)` yields futures in finishing order, so you can process results or submit follow-up work as soon as each is done. That suits searches, simulations and pipelines with dynamic structure.
- `future.status`, `future.exception()` and `future.cancel()` manage state and errors.

Results stay in worker memory as long as a Future referencing them exists in your Python program. Delete references, or let them go out of scope, to free the workers' memory.

`client.scatter(big_object)` sends data to the workers once, returning a Future you pass to many tasks instead of shipping the object with every call.

By default `submit` assumes **pure** functions: identical calls get the same key and are computed once. Pass `pure=False` for functions with randomness or side effects.
concepts.code:
import time
from dask.distributed import Client, as_completed

def slow_square(x):
    time.sleep(0.2 * (5 - x))      # later inputs finish sooner
    return x * x

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with Client(n_workers=1, threads_per_worker=5, processes=False) as client:
        futures = client.map(slow_square, range(5))
        order = [f.result() for f in as_completed(futures)]
        print(order)                       # [16, 9, 4, 1, 0]  (finish order)

        total = client.submit(sum, futures)    # depends on futures, data stays on workers
        print(total.result())              # 30

        lookup = client.scatter({"a": 1, "b": 2})
        print(client.submit(lambda d, k: d[k], lookup, "b").result())   # 2
takeaways: `submit`/`map` start work immediately and return Futures
Pass Futures into other tasks to chain work without moving data home
`as_completed` handles results as they finish; delete Futures to free memory
pitfalls: Holding millions of Futures in a list, keeping all their results pinned in cluster memory.

quiz.q: You pass future_a as an argument to client.submit(f, future_a). Where does f get the data?
options: The worker running f fetches it from the worker that holds it
Your laptop downloads it then re-uploads it
f receives the Future object and must call result()
quiz.explain: Dask resolves Future arguments on the cluster, moving data directly between workers.

concepts.name: Joins and shuffles at scale
concepts.summary: Understand when merges, sorts and set_index cause an all-to-all shuffle, and use broadcast and index-aligned joins to avoid it.
concepts.why: Shuffles are the most expensive thing a distributed DataFrame does, and choosing the right join strategy can change runtimes by orders of magnitude.
concepts.body:
Many-partition data has to be **shuffled** whenever rows with the same key must end up in the same partition: merges on non-index columns, `set_index`, `sort_values`, `groupby().apply`, `drop_duplicates` with `split_out`. A shuffle moves almost every row between partitions, over the network when workers are on different machines, and its cost grows with data size.

Dask chooses a merge strategy based on what it knows:

- **Broadcast join**: if one side is small (or has one partition), it is sent to every partition of the big side. No shuffle. You can force it with `broadcast=True` or by `repartition(npartitions=1)` on the small table.
- **Index-aligned join**: if both sides are indexed with known, compatible divisions, partitions are joined pairwise. No shuffle.
- **Hash shuffle join**: otherwise both sides are partitioned by hashing the key, then joined partition by partition.

On a distributed cluster the default shuffle method is **P2P** (peer-to-peer), which sends data between workers piece by piece as it is produced, keeps memory use bounded, and writes to disk when memory fills up. It is far more robust than the older task-based shuffle, which creates a number of tasks that grows with the square of the partition count.

Tactics: filter and select columns before merging, merge small dimension tables by broadcast, pre-partition data by a frequently joined key and save it with divisions, and avoid `sort_values` unless you really need global order.
concepts.code:
import dask.dataframe as dd
import pandas as pd

facts = dd.from_pandas(pd.DataFrame({
    "uid": [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3] * 5, "amount": range(30)}), npartitions=5)
users = pd.DataFrame({"uid": [1, 2, 3], "country": ["NO", "SE", "NO"]})

# Small pandas side: Dask broadcasts it to every partition (no shuffle)
joined = facts.merge(dd.from_pandas(users, npartitions=1), on="uid", how="left")
print(joined.npartitions)                       # 5
print(joined.groupby("country").amount.sum().compute().sort_index().to_dict())
# {'NO': 290, 'SE': 145}

# Two large sides on a non-index key: hash shuffle
other = dd.from_pandas(pd.DataFrame({"uid": [1, 2, 3] * 4, "score": range(12)}),
                       npartitions=4)
big = facts.merge(other, on="uid", shuffle_method="tasks")
print(len(big))                                 # 120
takeaways: Merges on non-index keys, `set_index` and sorts cause shuffles
Broadcast small tables; align on known divisions to avoid shuffling
The P2P shuffle on distributed is the robust default
pitfalls: Merging two huge tables before filtering them, shuffling data you'll throw away.

options: Two 1 TB tables on a non-index column
A 1 TB table with a 5 MB single-partition table
quiz.explain: A small single-partition table can be broadcast to every partition of the large one.

concepts.name: persist, memory and the dashboard
concepts.summary: Keep reused data in worker memory with persist, understand worker memory limits and spilling, and diagnose problems in the dashboard.
concepts.why: Memory pressure causes most failed Dask jobs, and persist plus the dashboard are how you control and see it.
concepts.body:
`df = df.persist()` starts computing a collection on the workers and keeps the results in **worker memory**, returning a collection backed by those in-memory pieces. Use it when you will reuse the same intermediate data many times, as in interactive exploration or methods that loop over the same data many times. `compute()` instead brings the result back to your process.

Persist only what fits comfortably in the workers' combined memory. Each worker has a `memory_limit` and reacts in stages: around 60% of the limit it **spills** data (moves some of it to disk to make room), around 70% it also spills based on process memory, at 80% it **pauses** accepting new tasks, and at 95% the nanny **restarts** the worker, losing its data. Frequent spilling or restarts mean partitions are too large, too much is persisted, or a task creates huge intermediate objects.

The **dashboard** (`client.dashboard_link`) shows this live:

- Task stream: a timeline of which task ran on which worker; red bars are time spent sending data, white gaps are idle time.
- Worker memory bars: grey for managed memory, orange for spilled, with the limit marked.
- Progress, graph and profile pages to find slow functions.

`client.get_task_stream()` and `performance_report(filename=...)` save diagnostics for later. Use `wait(df)` to block until a persist finishes, and `del df` or `client.cancel(df)` to release memory.
concepts.code:
import dask.dataframe as dd
import pandas as pd
from dask.distributed import Client, performance_report, wait

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with Client(n_workers=2, threads_per_worker=1, memory_limit="1GB") as client:
        pdf = pd.DataFrame({"k": [i % 10 for i in range(100_000)],
                            "v": range(100_000)})
        df = dd.from_pandas(pdf, npartitions=10)

        clean = df[df.v % 3 == 0].persist()   # computed once, kept on workers
        wait(clean)
        mem = client.run(lambda dask_worker: len(dask_worker.data))
        print(sum(mem.values()))              # 10  (partitions held in memory)

        with performance_report(filename="report.html"):   # needs bokeh
            print(clean.v.sum().compute())    # 1666683333
            print(clean.groupby("k").v.mean().compute().round().iloc[0])   # 49995.0
        del clean                             # frees worker memory
takeaways: `persist()` keeps computed partitions on workers for reuse
Workers spill, pause and restart at rising memory thresholds
The dashboard's task stream and memory bars explain most problems
pitfalls: Persisting a dataset larger than the workers' combined memory and causing constant spilling or worker restarts.

quiz.q: What's the difference between compute() and persist() on a Dask DataFrame?
options: compute returns a pandas result to the client; persist keeps a Dask collection whose partitions live in worker memory
quiz.explain: persist materializes data on the cluster for reuse, while compute brings a concrete result home.

concepts.name: The DataFrame query optimizer
concepts.summary: See how Dask DataFrame's expression system optimizes queries with projection and predicate pushdown, and inspect plans with pprint and explain.
concepts.why: Knowing what the optimizer can and can't rewrite helps you write code that it speeds up automatically.
concepts.body:
Since 2025, Dask DataFrame is built on an **expression system** (originally the `dask-expr` project). Each operation creates an expression node, and before running, Dask optimizes the whole expression tree, much like a database plans a query before running it.

Optimizations include:

- **Projection pushdown**: only columns used later are read from Parquet or kept through the pipeline.
- **Predicate pushdown**: filters move toward the reader, where Parquet filters can skip row groups.
- **Partition squashing**: after `read_parquet`, small files may be combined into fewer partitions automatically.
- **Merge and groupby planning**: choosing broadcast joins or tree reductions from size estimates.
- **Blockwise fusion**: chains of per-partition operations are fused into single tasks, which shrinks the graph.

Inspect it with `df.pprint()` for the raw expression tree, `df.optimize().pprint()` for the optimized one (`fuse=False` keeps fused steps readable), and `df.explain()` for a graphviz drawing (needs the `graphviz` package).

The optimizer works best when it can see the whole query. Opaque steps limit it: `map_partitions` with arbitrary functions, calling `compute()` midway, or converting to delayed objects. Write the query fully, then compute once.
concepts.code:
import dask.dataframe as dd
import pandas as pd

pd.DataFrame({"a": range(10), "b": list("xyxyxyxyxy"),
              "c": [1.0] * 10, "d": ["unused"] * 10}).to_parquet("t.parquet")

df = dd.read_parquet("t.parquet")
q = df[df.a > 2].groupby("b").a.sum()

q.optimize(fuse=False).pprint()
# Sum(TreeReduce): split_every=8
#   Sum(GroupByChunk): chunk=<methodcaller: sum> columns=a ...
#     Filter:
#       FusedIO:
#         ReadParquetFSSpec: path='t.parquet' columns=['a', 'b']
#       GT: right=2
#         Projection: columns='a'
#           FusedIO:
#             ReadParquetFSSpec: path='t.parquet' columns=['a', 'b']
print(q.compute().sort_index().to_dict())   # {'x': 18, 'y': 24}
takeaways: Dask DataFrame optimizes the whole expression before running
Projection and predicate pushdown reach into `read_parquet`
`optimize().pprint()` shows the plan; opaque steps limit optimization
pitfalls: Calling `.compute()` or `.persist()` mid-pipeline 'to be safe', which splits the query the optimizer could have improved.

quiz.q: In the plan above, why does the Parquet read list only columns ['a', 'b']?
options: The file has only two columns
groupby drops other columns after reading
Projection pushdown determined that c and d are never used
quiz.explain: The optimizer pushes the needed column set into the reader, so c and d are never loaded.

concepts.name: Task graphs and the graph spec
concepts.summary: Look under the hood: Dask's task graph specification, keys, low-level graphs from collections, fusion and ordering.
concepts.why: Understanding graphs lets you find the cause of slowness, build custom collections and reason about memory use.
concepts.body:
Every Dask collection ultimately produces a **task graph**: a mapping from **keys** to **tasks**. Keys are strings or tuples like `("sum-chunk-abc123", 0)`, typically one per partition. A task is a function call whose arguments may reference other keys. In recent versions tasks are `Task` objects from `dask._task_spec`; in older code they were tuples like `(func, arg1, arg2)`. You can still pass a plain dict graph to a scheduler: `dask.get(graph, key)`.

Collections implement the **Dask collection protocol**, an agreed set of methods: `__dask_graph__()`, `__dask_keys__()`, `__dask_optimize__` and `__dask_postcompute__`. That's what lets `dask.compute` handle DataFrames, Arrays, Delayed objects and third-party collections like xarray together and merge their graphs.

Before running, the scheduler side does more work:

- **Culling** drops tasks not needed for the requested keys.
- **Fusion** merges linear chains of tasks into one to cut overhead.
- **Ordering** (`dask.order`) picks an execution order that releases intermediate results early, which keeps memory low. Many memory blowups are ordering problems on unusual graph shapes.

Graph size is a cost in itself: building, sending and scheduling a graph of 10 million tasks takes noticeable time on the client and scheduler. Reduce task counts with bigger partitions, fused operations and fewer intermediate steps.
concepts.code:
import dask
from operator import add, mul

# A raw graph: keys map to values or tasks (func, *args); args can be keys
graph = {
    "x": 1,
    "y": 2,
    "sum": (add, "x", "y"),
    "out": (mul, "sum", 10),
    "unused": (mul, "y", 100),
}
print(dask.get(graph, "out"))           # 30  (synchronous scheduler)

@dask.delayed
def inc(i):
    return i + 1

total = dask.delayed(sum)([inc(i) for i in range(3)])
g = dict(total.__dask_graph__())
print(len(g))                           # 4  (three inc tasks + sum)
print(total.key.startswith("sum-"))     # True
print(dask.compute(total)[0])           # 6
takeaways: A graph maps keys to values or tasks that reference other keys
Collections expose graphs via the `__dask_graph__` protocol
Culling, fusion and ordering shape speed and memory
pitfalls: Ignoring graph size: tens of millions of tasks can take minutes before any computation starts.

quiz.q: Why does Dask's task ordering matter for memory?
options: Running tasks in an order that consumes intermediate results soon lets them be freed early
It doesn't; only the number of workers does
Ordering decides which columns are read
quiz.explain: A good order finishes dependents quickly so intermediate data can be released instead of piling up.

concepts.name: Inside the distributed scheduler
concepts.summary: Understand the scheduler, workers and client, task states, data locality, work stealing and resilience in dask.distributed.
concepts.why: When a large job stalls or behaves oddly, you need a mental model of how the scheduler places tasks and moves data.
concepts.body:
A distributed cluster has three roles. The **client** in your Python program builds graphs and sends them over. The **scheduler** is a single process that tracks every task's state and decides where it runs. **Workers** execute tasks in thread pools, store results in memory, and fetch dependencies directly from each other. A **nanny** process supervises each worker and restarts it if it dies or exceeds memory limits.

Each task moves through states on the scheduler: `released`, `waiting` (dependencies not ready), `processing` (assigned to a worker), `memory` (result held by a worker), or `erred`. Workers keep their own matching set of states and transitions.

Placement decisions:

- **Data locality**: a task usually goes to the worker that already holds most of its input bytes, estimating transfer cost from data sizes and how fast the network between workers is.
- **Queuing**: root tasks such as file reads are queued on the scheduler and released as workers free up, which keeps memory steady.
- **Work stealing**: idle workers take queued tasks from busy ones when the compute saved exceeds the transfer cost.

**Resilience**: if a worker dies, the scheduler recomputes lost results from the graph's lineage. A task that keeps killing workers is marked as erred after `allowed-failures` attempts (default 3), with a `KilledWorker` error. The usual cause is a task that uses too much memory.

The scheduler is single-threaded Python, so very high task rates, roughly thousands per second, make it the bottleneck. That's another reason to keep tasks coarse.
concepts.code:
from dask.distributed import Client

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with Client(n_workers=2, threads_per_worker=1, processes=False) as client:
        a = client.submit(lambda: list(range(100_000)), key="big-data")
        b = client.submit(len, a, key="needs-big")     # goes where 'big-data' lives
        print(b.result())                               # 100000

        who_has = client.who_has([a, b])
        print(who_has["big-data"] == who_has["needs-big"])   # True (data locality)

        info = client.scheduler_info()
        print(len(info["workers"]))                     # 2
        states = client.run_on_scheduler(
            lambda dask_scheduler: dask_scheduler.tasks["needs-big"].state)
        print(states)                                   # memory
takeaways: Client builds graphs; one scheduler tracks task states; workers compute and share data
Placement favours data locality, with queuing and work stealing to balance load
Lost results are recomputed; repeated crashes surface as KilledWorker
pitfalls: Seeing KilledWorker and retrying blindly instead of shrinking the memory used per task.

quiz.q: A task repeatedly causes its worker to be restarted. What does the scheduler eventually report?
options: KilledWorker after the allowed number of failures
quiz.explain: After distributed.scheduler.allowed-failures retries, the task errs with KilledWorker.

concepts.name: Deploying and scaling clusters
concepts.summary: Run Dask beyond a laptop on Kubernetes, HPC job queues, cloud VMs or managed services, with adaptive scaling and consistent environments.
concepts.why: Production Dask means picking a deployment that fits your infrastructure and keeping software identical on every machine.
concepts.body:
Every deployment starts the same three pieces, a scheduler, workers and your client, through different **cluster managers** with a shared interface: `cluster.scale(n)`, `cluster.adapt(minimum=, maximum=)`, `Client(cluster)`.

- **Local**: `LocalCluster`, one machine.
- **Kubernetes**: the `dask-kubernetes` operator with `KubeCluster`, or a Helm chart for a long-lived cluster.
- **HPC**: `dask-jobqueue` (`SLURMCluster`, `PBSCluster`, etc.) submits workers as batch jobs.
- **Cloud VMs**: `dask-cloudprovider` (EC2, Azure, GCP) or managed services such as Coiled.
- **Manual**: run `dask scheduler` and `dask worker tcp://host:8786` yourself, or use `SSHCluster`.

**Adaptive scaling** (`cluster.adapt(minimum=2, maximum=50)`) lets the scheduler request more workers when work is queued and release idle ones, saving money on bursty workloads.

Pitfalls specific to clusters:

- **Environment drift**: the client, scheduler and workers must have the same versions of Dask, Python and every library your tasks use. `client.get_versions(check=True)` checks. Build one software environment (for example one container image) and use it everywhere.

- **Data access**: workers read files themselves, so paths must be reachable from every worker. That means cloud object storage or a shared network drive, not your laptop's disk.

- **Security**: turn on encrypted connections (TLS) between the pieces, and don't expose the scheduler's network port to the public internet.

- **Configuration** lives in YAML files or environment variables like `DASK_DISTRIBUTED__WORKER__MEMORY__TARGET`, readable via `dask.config.get`.
concepts.code:
import dask
from dask.distributed import Client, LocalCluster

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # The same pattern works with KubeCluster, SLURMCluster, EC2Cluster...
    with LocalCluster(n_workers=0, threads_per_worker=1, processes=False) as cluster:
        cluster.adapt(minimum=1, maximum=3)   # scale with demand
        with Client(cluster) as client:
            client.wait_for_workers(1)
            print(len(client.scheduler_info()["workers"]) >= 1)    # True
            versions = client.get_versions(check=True)   # raises on mismatch
            print("python" in versions["scheduler"]["host"])     # True

            print(dask.config.get("distributed.scheduler.allowed-failures"))   # 3
            print(client.submit(sum, [1, 2, 3]).result())    # 6
takeaways: Cluster managers share one interface: scale, adapt, Client(cluster)
Keep identical environments on client, scheduler and workers
Workers read data themselves: use storage every worker can reach
pitfalls: Reading local file paths that exist only on the client machine from remote workers.

quiz.q: Tasks fail on workers with ModuleNotFoundError, but the same code works on your laptop. Most likely cause?
options: The scheduler is out of memory
The worker environment doesn't match the client's installed libraries
quiz.explain: Workers import the functions' dependencies themselves, so their environment must include the same packages.
